road.name: Touchet Road / FR-64 (Bluewood Road) from Dayton
road.status: Paved North Touchet Road out of Dayton becomes gravel-to-dirt Forest Service Road 64 at the forest boundary as it climbs toward the Bluewood ski area; the climbing dikes sit right along this road roughly 16-17 miles in (about 1-2 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead). Approach paths to individual crags (Megadike, Minidike, Weeping Wall, Joe's Rock) are unofficial, brushy, and easy to lose.
road.driveNote: Roughly 25-30 minutes (about 20 miles) from Dayton, WA via S 4th Street/North Touchet Road (FR-64).
road.seasonalGate: The upper Touchet/FR-64 corridor toward Bluewood is only reliably snow-free roughly mid-June through October; expect snow to block it in winter and spring.

before.approach: The Dikes sit in the Umatilla National Forest's Walla Walla Ranger District, in the East Fork Touchet River valley near Ski Bluewood, southeast Washington — not near the Snake River. Access is via North Touchet Road out of Dayton, WA, paved for roughly the first 15-16 miles before becoming gravel Forest Service Road 64 at the forest boundary; the road is passable roughly April-November and can hold snow into early summer. Approaches are very short and roadside: the south Megadike is reached by parking near a bridge 1.2 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead and scrambling directly up the steep hillside above the bridge abutment, while Weeping Wall and Joe's Rock are similar short pullout-to-cliff scrambles at 1.1 and 2.0 miles past the same trailhead respectively. The area is lightly visited and faint-trailed, and the basalt is notably loose/fractured, requiring routine loose-rock cleaning. This route is on Megadike North: park 1.1 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead, where a dirt road intersects the paved road on the left (SE side), or continue to 1.2 miles and use the large pull-off. Cross the main road and pick up the approach trail between the two parking spots, marked by a short steep drainage topped with a downed tree.

waypoints.name: Middle Point Ridge Trailhead
waypoints.note: FS Rd 64 trailhead (vault toilet, no water) on the East Fork Touchet River; head upstream/south toward Bluewood to reach The Dikes basalt fins.
waypoints.directions: From Dayton, follow North Touchet Road up the East Fork Touchet River valley toward Ski Bluewood; it stays paved for roughly the first 15 to 16 miles, then turns to gravel as Forest Service Road 64 at the forest boundary. The Middle Point Ridge Trailhead sits on the river at about 3,373 feet, with a vault toilet and no water. The road is generally passable from about April to November and can hold snow into early summer, so expect a later opening in a heavy year. The Dikes lie farther on, upstream and south toward Bluewood.

waypoints.name: Megadike North
waypoints.note: Tallest fin of The Dikes (walls to 120 ft); park ~1.1 mi past the trailhead at a pulloff/dirt-road junction, then follow the short steep drainage trail (marked by a downed tree) to the base.

before.best_season: April-November per USFS season of use.

before.watch_out:
Occasionally loose rock throughout—typical of Dikes granite; variable rock quality requires cautious climbing; always test holds and placements
No continuous crack systems—protection limited and often minimal; runouts between protection; bold climbing required
Exposed arete climbing—significant consequence if protection fails; narrow ridge exposure with drops on both sides; maintains climber focus requirement
Dirty/mossy sections possible—rock quality variable season-to-season; lichen growth and moisture affect climbing texture; clean before climbing if needed
Route-finding complexity on arete variations—multiple lines possible; easy to wander off established route; study topo and photos
Weather exposure on open ridge—afternoon thunderstorms common in eastern Cascades; exposed to wind and lightning; start early
Descent route-finding—rappel anchor locations must be confirmed; two-rope descent may be necessary; descent terrain exposed
Lower altitude but exposed position—7000+ ft elevation gain from trailhead; sustained climbing with exposure; fatigue on descent increases risk
